case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Georgia Department of Human Services v. Spruill
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the Court of Appeals and held that the Georgia Tort Claims Act's discretionary function exception preserved sovereign immunity for a DFCS caseworker's choices in investigating a report of child neglect, barring the tort suit brought after the children were severely injured.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading Georgia case on the discretion exercised when a screened report is escalated to investigation.
key_cases.quote: But when such agents act as representatives of the sovereign, they exercise a different sort of discretion, one that may be informed in significant part by considerations of public policy.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal on qualified immunity, holding that social workers who interviewed a minor without her father's consent and threatened removal during a child abuse investigation violated no clearly established Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment right.
key_cases.relevance: It addresses what investigators may do once a report is escalated to a full child abuse investigation.
key_cases.quote: Because neither social worker violated any clearly established federal civil rights in the investigation that Loftus had invited, we affirm the dismissal of Loftus's complaint against them.

key_cases.case_name: Georgia Department of Human Services, Division of Family and Children Services v. Steiner
key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia reversed the superior court and upheld the central child abuse registry as applied, holding that listing as a substantiated abuser did not, on this record, satisfy the stigma-plus test and so triggered no federal procedural due process protection, and that 'some evidence' supported the ALJ's substantiation.
key_cases.relevance: It maps the escalation from report to investigation to substantiation and administrative review.
key_cases.quote: Steiner failed to demonstrate a constitutionally protected liberty or property interest sufficient to trigger the due process protections that he claims were violated by operation of the registry

key_cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed a declaratory judgment striking down Georgia's former central child abuse registry, holding that a person classified as a confirmed abuser has more than a reputational interest at stake and that the statute's absolute bar on compelling testimony from a child under 14 denies due process in a large fraction of cases, so the entire Act, OCGA 49-5-180 et seq., had to fall.
key_cases.relevance: It sets out in detail the statutory path from completed investigation through the unfounded, unconfirmed and confirmed classifications and the administrative hearing that follows.
key_cases.quote: The portion of OCGA § 49-5-183.1 that precludes an accused from compelling a child's testimony in the administrative proceedings is unconstitutional and central to the general scope of the Act

mandatory_reporters: Physicians licensed to practice medicine, physician assistants, interns, or residents — O.C.G.A. § 19-7-5(c)(1)
Licensed psychologists and persons in internships to obtain licensure (O.C.G.A. Title 43, Ch. 39)
Registered professional nurses, licensed practical nurses (O.C.G.A. Title 43, Ch. 26), or nurse's aides
Professional counselors, social workers, or marriage and family therapists (O.C.G.A. Title 43, Ch. 10A)
School counselors, visiting teachers, school social workers, or school psychologists (O.C.G.A. Title 20, Ch. 2)
Child welfare agency personnel (as defined in O.C.G.A. § 49-5-12)

Child service organization personnel — anyone employed by or volunteering at an organization that provides care, treatment, education, training, supervision, coaching, counseling, recreational programs, or shelter to children (O.C.G.A. § 19-7-5(b)(6))
Reproductive health care facility or pregnancy resource center personnel and volunteers
Clergy — must report unless the information was received solely within confession or a similar communication required to be kept confidential under church doctrine (O.C.G.A. § 19-7-5(g))
reporting_details: Georgia is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals listed in O.C.G.A. § 19-7-5(c)(1) — plus clergy outside the confessional under § 19-7-5(g) — must report suspected child abuse, orally or in writing, immediately and in no case later than 24 hours (§ 19-7-5(e)(2)), while any other person may report but is not required to (§ 19-7-5(d)).

abuse: Physical injury or death inflicted upon a child by a parent, guardian, legal custodian, or other person responsible for the care of such child by other than accidental means; provided, however, that physical forms of discipline may be used as long as there is no physical injury to the child (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(A))
Neglect of a child by a parent, guardian, legal custodian, or other person responsible for the care of such child (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(B))
Sexual abuse or sexual exploitation of a child (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(D))
Prenatal abuse of a child by a parent (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(E))
An act or failure to act that presents an imminent risk of serious harm to the child's physical, mental, or emotional health (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(F))
Trafficking a child for labor servitude (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(5)(G))
neglect: The failure to provide proper parental care or control, subsistence, education as required by law, or other care or control necessary for a child's physical, mental, or emotional health or morals (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(11)(A))
The failure to provide a child with adequate supervision necessary for such child's well-being (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(11)(B))
The abandonment of a child by his or her parent, guardian, or legal custodian (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(11)(C))
other: "Child" means any person under 18 years of age (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(4))

"Emotional abuse" means acts or omissions by a parent, guardian, legal custodian, or other person responsible for the care of a child that cause any mental injury to such child's intellectual or psychological capacity as evidenced by an observable and significant impairment in such child's ability to function within a child's normal range of performance and behavior or that create a substantial risk of impairment (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(8))

"Person responsible for the care of a child" means an adult member of a child's household; a person exercising supervision over a child for any part of the 24 hour day; or any adult who, based on his or her relationship to the parent, guardian, or legal custodian or a member of a child's household, has access to such child (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(12))
substance_related: Prenatal abuse: exposure to chronic or severe use of alcohol or the unlawful use of any controlled substance (as defined in O.C.G.A. 16-13-21) which results in symptoms of withdrawal in a newborn or the presence of a controlled substance or a metabolite thereof in a newborn's body, blood, urine, or meconium that is not the result of medical treatment (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(14)(A))

Prenatal abuse: exposure to chronic or severe use of alcohol or the unlawful use of any controlled substance (as defined in O.C.G.A. 16-13-21) which results in medically diagnosed and harmful effects in a newborn's physical appearance or functioning (O.C.G.A. 19-7-5(b)(14)(B))

timeline_requirements.deadline: Immediate (present danger); 24 hours (impending danger); 5 weekdays (abuse indicated, no safety threat)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in policy; the assigned window is the maximum time allowed to make face-to-face purposeful contact with the alleged victim child
Not specified in policy; the investigation must also be submitted to and approved by the Social Services Supervisor within the same 45 calendar days
